c.tagline: Central Asia's ancient Silk Road capital, reborn modern.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis usually negotiate a fixed price before departure; ride-hailing apps like Yandex Go show an upfront fare and are the more reliable, safer option.

emergency.note: Unified mobile emergency number 112 also works; fire brigade is 101.

avoid.reason: Watch for taxi overcharging and petty theft at Chorsu Bazaar, and carry your passport as police document checks occur.

hood_desc: The modern, business-oriented heart of the city around Amir Timur Square, packed with international hotels, government buildings, and museums; ideal for first-time visitors who want everything within walking distance.
A leafy, upscale district of wide avenues, shopping malls, and the striking blue-domed Minor Mosque; suits travelers who prefer a quieter, more residential base with easy metro access.
The atmospheric Old City around Chorsu Bazaar, with narrow lanes, madrasas, and the vast domed market; best for travelers chasing an authentic, traditional Uzbek atmosphere.
A green, academic and diplomatic quarter served by its own metro stop, home to embassies and the national university; good for a calmer stay still close to the center.
A central, well-connected residential district near the main railway station, favored by budget travelers and longer-stay visitors for its guesthouses and value hotels.

water.note: Avoid tap water; stick to bottled or boiled water.

transit.pay: Metro and most city buses use the contactless ATTO smart card (also loadable with mobile wallets like Apple/Google Pay), tapped at turnstiles or validators; cash is still accepted for a single metro ride (3,000 som) at station counters. Tourists can buy an ATTO card at any metro station.
transit.hours: Metro operates roughly 5:00-24:00 daily; buses run similar hours with reduced frequency late at night; no all-night service.
transit.note: The metro (opened 1977, the first in Central Asia) has 4 lines and is clean, cheap, and a tourist attraction in itself for its ornate Soviet-era stations.

train: Tashkent Railway Station (Afrosiyob high-speed trains to Samarkand/Bukhara, Sharq express trains)
bus: Intercity/regional buses from Tashkent bus terminals

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus (~40 min to center)

tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 5-10% in restaurants is appreciated but not obligatory; tipping taxi drivers is uncommon.

food.name: Plov
food.desc: Uzbekistan's national rice dish - lamb, carrots and rice cooked in huge kazan cauldrons, topped with quail egg or horse sausage if you dare.

places.name: Besh Qozon (Central Asian Plov Centre)
places.note: Giant cauldrons feed thousands daily; Lonely Planet-recommended - go before early afternoon

places.name: KamolonOsh Drujba
places.note: Locals' pick for Samarkand-style plov in the capital

food.name: Lagman
food.desc: Hand-pulled noodles in a peppery lamb and vegetable broth - the Uyghur-Uzbek comfort bowl found in every bazaar.

places.name: Chorsu Bazaar food hall
places.note: Second-floor hall where locals eat elbow-to-elbow; bowls for 15,000-30,000 som

places.name: Afsona
places.note: Modern takes on Uzbek classics, praised by recent travel writers

food.name: Samsa
food.desc: Flaky lamb-and-onion pastries blistered on the walls of a tandoor oven - Tashkent's best cheap snack, eaten hot with vinegar.

places.name: Chorsu Bazaar tandoor stalls
places.note: Watch samsa slapped onto the clay oven walls; a few thousand som each

places.name: Caravan
places.note: Its flaky mini samsa with juicy meat filling get repeated praise

food.name: Shashlik
food.desc: Skewers of lamb ribs, minced kofta or chicken grilled over saxaul wood - the smoky centerpiece of an Uzbek evening.

places.name: Chigatoy Shashlik
places.note: Old-recipe marinated skewers; a repeated local recommendation

places.name: Shashleek Eco Park
places.note: Garden setting with some of the city's best-reviewed skewers

food.name: Manti
food.desc: Big steamed dumplings of hand-chopped lamb and onion, eaten with sour cream - grandmother food, Tashkent-style.

places.name: MANDU
places.note: A specialist that serves only manti, in many fillings

places.name: Chorsu Bazaar stalls
places.note: Manti and rolled khanum from the bazaar's cheap food rows

food.name: Green tea (kok-choy)
food.desc: Pots of green tea poured three times into small piala bowls - the ritual that anchors every chaikhana (teahouse) meal.

places.name: Chorsu Bazaar chaikhanas
places.note: Pots of kok-choy are the bazaar ritual between shopping rounds

places.name: Plov Poytaxt
places.note: Popular, very affordable choyxona; tea accompanies every plate of plov

food.name: Kompot and ayran
food.desc: House-made fruit kompot and salty yogurt ayran - the traditional coolers served alongside plov and grilled meat.

places.name: Afsona
places.note: Seasonal fruit kompot alongside its modern Uzbek menu

places.name: Caravan
places.note: Ayran and kompot poured with grills on the summer terraces

landmarks: Khast Imam Complex
A revered religious complex housing the ancient Uthman Quran, its grand mosques and madrasahs forming the spiritual center of Islamic Tashkent.
Chorsu Bazaar
A bustling bazaar beneath a massive turquoise dome, where vendors sell spices, dried fruit, and crafts in one of Central Asia's liveliest markets.
Amir Timur Square
A leafy central square anchored by an equestrian statue of Timur, surrounded by elegant colonial and Soviet-era architecture.
Tashkent TV Tower
A soaring 375-meter tower and one of the tallest structures in Central Asia, offering an observation deck with panoramic city views.
Independence Square (Mustaqillik Maydoni)
Uzbekistan's largest public square, featuring the Independence Monument, fountains, and the symbolic Arch of Good and Noble Aspirations.
Kosmonavtlar Metro Station
A dazzling Soviet-era metro station decorated with cosmic murals and portraits honoring space pioneers, often called one of the world's most beautiful subway stops.
Minor Mosque
A gleaming white marble mosque built in 2014 on the banks of the Bozsu Canal, notable for its striking blue domes and modern grandeur.
Alisher Navoi Opera and Ballet Theatre
A grand Soviet-built theater decorated with regional artistic motifs from across Uzbekistan, still hosting world-class opera and ballet performances.
Kukeldash Madrasah
A 16th-century Islamic school with an imposing tiled facade, standing beside Chorsu Bazaar as one of Tashkent's finest surviving historic monuments.
State Museum of History of Uzbekistan
A major national museum tracing millennia of Uzbek history through archaeological treasures, ancient manuscripts, and cultural artifacts.

train.note: International and domestic trains leave from Tashkent (Toshkent) central station. The Tashkent-Almaty service is a modern Talgo sleeper running every few days via the Kazakh border. The long Tashkent-Moscow train (via Kazakhstan) mainly serves labour migrants and takes about three days. Switch the eticket.railway.uz site to English (top right). HUMAN EDITOR: reconfirm the Tashkent-Moscow train is still selling for 2026.

intl.op: shared taxis and marshrutka minibuses — depart from the Kuyluk and northern bus stations, no online booking

bus.note: International travel from Tashkent is mostly by shared taxi and marshrutka (minibus) rather than scheduled coaches with online booking: frequent departures to Shymkent and Almaty (Kazakhstan), Bishkek (Kyrgyzstan) and Khujand (Tajikistan) leave from Tashkent's bus stations (e.g. the northern/Kuyluk areas). Buy on the spot; carry your passport for border checks.

ferry.note: Tashkent and Uzbekistan are doubly landlocked, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Charvak Reservoir
half.blurb: A turquoise mountain lake popular for swimming, boating and summer lakeside escapes.

half.name: Chimgan Mountains
half.blurb: Rugged peaks offering hiking, cable-car rides and winter skiing near the capital.

half.name: Samarkand
half.blurb: A legendary Silk Road city of turquoise domes, madrasas and grand Registan square.

half.name: Khodjikent
half.blurb: A riverside foothill village near cable cars, petroglyphs and mountain scenery.

full.name: Kokand
full.blurb: A historic khanate capital with an ornate palace and centuries-old mosques.

full.name: Fergana Valley
full.blurb: A fertile valley renowned for silk weaving, ceramics and traditional craft towns.
